findings.text: Mount descent helpers advance a mount-plus-dentry location down through mounted filesystems. One form attempts a single layer transition and reports whether movement occurred while transferring references to the new mount and its root. The other traverses a stack of mounts and releases the prior mount reference only when the mount changed.

A filesystem location is represented as a paired mount and dentry that are updated together during traversal. Movement preserves reachability by acquiring the destination references before releasing the source references.

Slow directory lookup can run under a shared, interruptible-by-fatal-signal directory lock. The lock is held only for the slow resolution interval and is always released before returning, with interruption reported as an intrrupt outcome.
Path-walk mode uses three small flag values: trailing-component handling is one, more-components handling is two, and no-follow handling is four.

Dot and dot-dot final-component sentinels have word-size-dependent encodings. One variant places dot and double-dot patterns at the high end of a machine word; the other uses compact low values for the same two names.

Parent-oriented resolution requires a normal final component and rejects other final-component types as invalid. On success it supplies both the resolved parent location and the final name or entry for subsequent directory mutation or lookup.

Full-path lookup helpers resolve a supplied pathname from either an explicit directory-plus-mount root or a descriptor-relative user pathname. Flags are propagated to the underlying filename resolution.

Name lookup separates permission-independent name handling from execute-permission checking on the parent. Cached resolution is preferred when available, with a slower authoritative path used on cache miss; unlocked forms do not assume the caller already holds the parent lock.
Two lookup forms require the caller to already hold the parent directory lock. Violation is treated as a programming warning rather than a normal error path.

Positive-only lookup variants convert a successfully resolved but negative entry into a missing-entry outcome after releasing the entry. Killable and unlocked forms differ only in blocking and locking assumptions, not in this polarity contract.

Directory mutation startup performs a preliminary name and permission check before beginning the protected directory operation. Creation startup requests create semantics while removal startup does not; permission-bypassing forms omit the execute check, and killable forms permit fatal-signal interruption while waiting.
Dentry-based mutation startup holds the parent directory in a nested parent lock on success. Failure paths release that lock before reporting an error.

Dentry-based mutation startup validates that the parent is alive, that the child remains hashed, and that the child still belongs to that parent. Creation requires absence and reports already-exists otherwise; removal requires presence and reports missing otherwise.

Terminal-device path assistance moves from an input location to its parent, resolves a sibling terminal-multiplexor name there, and then descends through any mount at that name. Unconnected parents and missing sibling entries are reported as missing.

Sticky-directory deletion authorization succeeds for the owner of either the containing directory or the target object. Otherwise it depends on ownership-override privilege evaluated against the target ownership context.

Rename locking uses a filesystem-wide rename mutex plus two nested parent locks when two distinct parents are involved. A single-parent rename takes only one nested parent lock and no global mutex; unlock always reverses acquisition, releasing directory locks before the global mutex when present.

Rename preparation detects ancestor relationships between source and target through a trap marker. A source that is an ancestor of the target is invalid; a target that is an ancestor of the source is invalid for exchange and reported as non-empty target otherwise. Disconnected parents without a common ancestor are reported as cross-device.

Rename target semantics depend on exchange and no-replace requests: exchange disables target-creation treatment, while no-replace adds exclusivity and rejects an existing positive target. Name-based forms check both names before locking; dentry-based forms revalidate hashed state and parent linkage after locking.

A rename source supplied as an already-resolved entry may move concurrently. The protocol therefore uses an optimistic same-parent fast path with fallback to the slow global-mutex path and revalidates parent identity after locks are held.

Generic object creation first authorizes creation in the parent, then constrains the requested mode to permission bits and forces regular-file type before invoking security authorization and the object-specific constructor. Success triggers creation notification; constructor failure does not.

Lookup-plus-open for regular files maps non-regular results to type-specific failures: directories, symlinks, device nodes, and fifo or socket objects each receive distinct error outcomes. It also enforces missing-entry and exclusive-create conflicts, and opens the file only when not already opened by lower layers.

Dentry-based file creation has two paths. When the parent supports combined lookup-and-open, that combined operation handles creation and opening with create and open notifications keyed to the resulting file state. Otherwise creation and opening are performed as separate ordered operations.

Kernel temporary-file opening allocates an unaccounted open file object with caller-supplied credentials and then instantiates an unnamed temporary file beneath the supplied parent. Instantiation failure releases the allocated file object.
Pathname-based creation startup accepts kernel-resident and user-resident pathname forms respectively. Both are descriptor-relative and propagate caller lookup flags to filename creation.

Special-file creation, directory creation, and directory removal system calls accept user pathnames and delegate to filename-oriented helpers. Forms without an explicit directory descriptor resolve relative to the current working directory.

Several paths transfer mount, dentry, or file ownership across layers. Correctness depends on releasing only superseded references, dropping negatively resolved entries after positive-only filtering, and returning allocated file objects without an extra release on success.
